{{Short description|Type of field in mathematics}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''p''-adically closed field}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''''p''-adically closed field''' is a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] that enjoys a closure property that is a close analogue for [[p-adic number|''p''-adic fields]] to what [[Real closed field|real closure]] is to the [[Real number|real field]].  They were introduced by [[James Ax]] and [[Simon B. Kochen]] in 1965.{{sfnp|Ax|Kochen|1965}}

== Definition ==

Let <math>K</math> be the field <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> of [[rational number]]s and <math>v</math> be its usual [[p-adic valuation|<math>p</math>-adic valuation]] (with <math>v(p)=1</math>).  If <math>F</math> is a (not necessarily [[algebraic extension|algebraic]]) [[Field extension|extension field]] of <math>K</math>, itself equipped with a [[Valuation (algebra)|valuation]] <math>w</math>, we say that <math>(F,w)</math> is '''formally ''p''-adic''' when the following conditions are satisfied:
* <math>w</math> extends <math>v</math> (that is, <math>w(x)=v(x)</math> for all <math>x\in K</math>),
* the [[residue field]] of <math>w</math> coincides with the residue field of <math>v</math> (the residue field being the quotient of the valuation ring <math>\{x\in F : w(x)\geq 0\}</math> by its [[maximal ideal]] <math>\{x\in F : w(x)>0\}</math>),
* the smallest positive value of <math>w</math> coincides with the smallest positive value of <math>v</math> (namely 1, since <math>v</math> was assumed to be normalized): in other words, a [[uniformizer]] for <math>K</math> remains a uniformizer for <math>F</math>.
Note that the value group of <math>K</math> may be larger than that of <math>F</math> since it may contain infinitely large elements over the latter.

Thus the formally <math>p</math>-adic fields can be viewed as an analogue of the [[formally real field]]s.

For example, the field <math>\Q(i)</math> of [[Gaussian rational]]s, if equipped with the valuation <math>w</math> given by <math>w(2+i)=1</math> (and <math>w(2-i)=0</math>) is formally 5-adic (the place <math>v=5</math> of the rationals splits in two places of the Gaussian rationals since <math>x^2+1</math> factors over the residue field with 5 elements, and <math>w</math> is one of these places).  The field of 5-adic numbers (which contains both the rationals and the Gaussian rationals embedded as per the place <math>w</math>) is also formally 5-adic.  On the other hand, the field of Gaussian rationals is ''not'' formally 3-adic for any valuation, because the only valuation <math>w</math> on it which extends the 3-adic valuation is given by <math>w(3)=1</math> and its residue field has 9 elements.

When <math>F</math> is formally <math>p</math>-adic but that there does not exist any proper ''algebraic'' formally <math>p</math>-adic extension of <math>F</math>, then <math>F</math> is said to be '''''p''-adically closed'''.  For example, the field of <math>p</math>-adic numbers is <math>p</math>-adically closed, and so is the [[algebraic closure]] of the rationals inside it (the field of <math>p</math>-adic algebraic numbers).

If <math>F</math> is <math>p</math>-adically closed, then{{sfnp|Jarden|Roquette|1980|loc=lemma 4.1}}
* there is a unique valuation <math>w</math> on <math>F</math> which makes <math>F</math> <math>p</math>-adically closed (so it is legitimate to say that <math>F</math>, rather than the pair <math>(F,w)</math>, is <math>p</math>-adically closed),
* <math>F</math> is [[Henselian ring|Henselian]] with respect to this place (that is, its valuation ring is so),
* the valuation ring of <math>F</math> is exactly the image of the Kochen operator (see [[#The Kochen operator|below]]),
* the value group of <math>F</math> is an extension by <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> (the value group of <math>K</math>) of a divisible group, with the [[lexicographical order]].
The first statement is an analogue of the fact that the order of a real-closed field is uniquely determined by the [[algebraic structure]].

The definitions given above can be copied to a more general context: if <math>K</math> is a field equipped with a valuation <math>v</math> such that
* the residue field of <math>K</math> is finite (call <math>q</math> its cardinality and <math>p</math> its characteristic),
* the value group of <math>v</math> admits a smallest positive element (call it 1, and say <math>\pi</math> is a uniformizer, i.e. <math>v(\pi)=1</math>),
* <math>K</math> has finite absolute ramification, i.e., <math>v(p)</math> is finite (that is, a finite multiple of <math>v(\pi)=1</math>),
then we can speak of formally <math>v</math>-adic fields (or <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-adic if <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is the ideal corresponding to <math>v</math>) and <math>v</math>-adically complete fields. These hypotheses are notably satisfied for the field of rationals, with the [[prime number]] <math>q=\pi=p</math> having valuation 1.

== The Kochen operator ==

If <math>K</math> is a field equipped with a valuation <math>v</math> satisfying the hypothesis and with the notations introduced in the previous paragraph, define the Kochen operator by
:<math>\gamma(z) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\frac{z^q-z}{(z^q-z)^2-1}</math>
(when <math>z^q-z \neq \pm 1</math>). It is easy to check that <math>\gamma(z)</math> always has non-negative valuation. The Kochen operator can be thought of as a <math>p</math>-adic (or <math>v</math>-adic) analogue of the square function in the real case.

An extension field <math>F</math> of <math>K</math> is formally <math>v</math>-adic [[if and only if]] <math>1/\pi</math> does not belong to the subring generated over the value ring of <math>K</math> by the image of the Kochen operator on <math>F</math>. This is an analogue of the statement that a field is formally real when <math>-1</math> is not a sum of squares.

== First-order theory ==

The first-order theory of <math>p</math>-adically closed fields (here we are restricting ourselves to the <math>p</math>-adic case, i.e., <math>K</math> is the field of rationals and <math>v</math> is the <math>p</math>-adic valuation) is [[Complete theory|complete]] and [[Model complete theory|model complete]], and if we slightly enrich the language it admits [[quantifier elimination]].  Thus, one can define <math>p</math>-adically closed fields as those whose first-order theory is [[elementarily equivalent]] to that of <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math>.
